original_value: In this article, we propose a novel deep Siamese architecture based on a convolutional neural network (CNN) and multi-level similarity perception for the person re-identification (re-ID) problem. According to the distinct characteristics of diverse feature maps, we effectively apply different similarity constraints to both low-level and high-level feature maps during training stage. Due to the introduction of appropriate similarity comparison mechanisms at different levels, the proposed approach can adaptively learn discriminative local and global feature representations, respectively, while the former is more sensitive in localizing part-level prominent patterns relevant to re-identifying people across cameras. Meanwhile, a novel strong activation pooling strategy is utilized on the last convolutional layer for abstract local-feature aggregation to pursue more representative feature representations. Based on this, we propose final feature embedding by simultaneously encoding original global features and discriminative local features. In addition, our framework has two other benefits: First, classification constraints can be easily incorporated into the framework, forming a unified multi-task network with similarity constraints. Second, as similarity-comparable information has been encoded in the network’s learning parameters via back-propagation, pairwise input is not necessary at test time. That means we can extract features of each gallery image and build an index in an off-line manner, which is essential for large-scale real-world applications. Experimental results on multiple challenging benchmarks demonstrate that our method achieves splendid performance compared with the current state-of-the-art approaches.

result.paraphrase: This article introduces a new deep Siamese CNN architecture with multi-level similarity perception for person re-identification (re-ID). Guided by the differing properties of feature maps at multiple depths, the training process applies distinct similarity constraints to both low-level and high-level maps. With suitable similarity-comparison mechanisms at each level, the method can adaptively learn discriminative local and global feature representations; the former is especially sensitive to part-level salient patterns useful for identifying people across cameras. It also uses a novel strong activation pooling strategy on the final convolutional layer to aggregate local features into more representative embeddings. On this basis, the final embedding encodes both original global features and discriminative local features simultaneously. The framework offers two additional advantages: classification constraints can be easily integrated, yielding a unified multi-task network with similarity constraints, and pairwise input is unnecessary at test time because similarity-comparable information is learned in the network parameters through back-propagation. Thus, features for each gallery image can be extracted and indexed offline, which is crucial for large-scale real-world use. Experiments on several challenging benchmarks show that the proposed method outperforms current state-of-the-art approaches.
